segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt, sitting in for Ira Glass. This all started with a phone call, a call that eventually led to this episode. So that's where I'm going to start. I was talking to a journalist in Gaza on the phone.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, this is Chana. Hi.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: How are you?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This was back in April. I'd been speaking to people in Gaza for months by then, but nobody where Maram was, in the middle area, Deir Balah. Maram Hamaid, she's a reporter for Al Jazeera English. We were chatting. I was asking some pretty basic questions about what she was experiencing, what she was seeing, what the day had been like. She got interrupted.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: It was a little bit calm day in Deir Balah. You know, like--

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Who is it, Mom?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: So Banias is listening. I need to introduce Banias to you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Banias.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How are you?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I'm fine, thank you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Maram and I kept talking-- or trying to.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And you're in Deir Balah? Are you in Deir Balah?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Now what do I do?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Yeah, we are in Deir Balah--

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Mom--

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: --in the central area.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: --now what do I do?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is that where you're from? Is that where your home is, or did you--

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Uh, no. I'm displaced.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: And we're living in our relative's home here, with around 80 other family members.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: "Ay-dee"!

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: It's "ay-dee," not "ay-tee." Not "ay-tee."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's a lot of people.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Yeah. Yeah, yeah. Like a big number--

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Mom, it's "ay-dee," not "ay-tee."

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: So Banias is correcting me regarding the American accent, OK? So she's saying, like, what is it? It's "ay-tee" or "ay-dee"?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: "Ay-dee"!

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Oh.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: "Ay-dee." "Ay-dee."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does she correct you a lot?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Yeah! A lot, a lot. She speaks English better than me because I started with her from very young.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Back to me.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: I'm here around Banias--

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Back to me.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Back to me. [LAUGHS] Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And where--

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: She's-- yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Does she want to talk?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah, I'm pretty ready. I'm ready, ready.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're ready, ready. How old are you, Banias?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I'm eight years old.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're eight years old. And where did you learn to speak like an American?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: From Mama.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Uh-huh. She speaks to you in English?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah. Do you hear that? Do you hear that wee-wee-wee?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I do. Yeah. What is it?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: So Banias is-- [SIGHS] what is it?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: It's the whoosh, whoosh, whoosh. A war plane.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's a warplane. I do hear it, yeah.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I, of course, hear it, because it never ends.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Banias then takes the phone from her mom-- having told me what they are hearing, begins pointing out what they're seeing, saying, look at this-- as if I can also see, even though we're not on a video call. She says, here we have the window, as you can see. Here's the curtains. There are flowers. We don't have any sofas, just-- Mom, how do you say it?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mattresses?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Just "may-tresses," as you can see. We sit sometimes on bed, on the ground. Women are covering their heads all the time, as you can see.

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: [LAUGHS] She couldn't see. You should tell her.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah, tell me.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: OK. Oh, did you see our room?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: If you see it, you will-- you will run, run, run, run from this.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Maram Hamaid
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Because it's so old and dusty.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Maram told me later she was so surprised at Banias's performance in this call. That was the word she used. Apparently, Banias was marching around with the phone in front of her, telling people, I need the room, please, jumping on the mattress, standing on the table, pointing, saying, here's my brother, Iyas.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: There he is. He's pretty and smart like me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Gaza is full of kids. About half the population is under 18 years old, and about half of that group is under 10 years old, like Banias. A huge way in which children in this war are different from kids in other war zones is that children in Gaza are not allowed to leave. They're not displaced to some other spot away from the fighting. They're displaced inside Gaza. They're stuck in the violence and stuck with their families, in crowded rooms or tents, doing the things that kids everywhere do, building their inner world, trying to make sense of the world around them. I was calling Maram that day to ask about the situation in Deir Balah, and Banias took the phone and said, no, no, no, don't ask her. Ask me.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Being in Deir a Balah is boring.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's boring?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Really boring.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Not just-- bored, so bored. I really miss the burgers. And now we are on canned food. We have just the boxes of food, the food boxes. One day-- I want to tell you something.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Tell me.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: One day, when we are sitting in our room talking about something, then boom! A big bomb broke all of the windows, and the home was shaking. And my baby brother, Iyas, has got injured in his head. We have noticed the glass in his head.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oof. Is he OK, Banias?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yes, now he's all right.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We talked for a while and then said goodbye. That was the end of April. And then, in July, I saw Maram's name on my phone.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi. Maram? Can you hear me? Hello?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It was Banias. She wanted to talk, tell me about her day. Then, another day.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Banias.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Do you want to talk to me?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah, sure. What are you doing?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Through the summer, into the fall, Banias called me, and I called her. Maram, her mother, gave permission for these phone calls, but it was always just Banias on the line, telling me about herself and her life. I wanted to know what it's like to be a kid in this war. And here was this kid who wanted to talk.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Banias was a natural narrator of her own life. She was constantly directing my attention. These are my friends. This is my school stationery, as you can see. Do you want to know what we're doing right now? I'll tell you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Unfortunately for me, she also had zero interest in satisfying my journalistic agenda. If I asked Banias a question she was not interested in, she'd yawn dramatically, stage yawn. [YAWNS] It's getting late. I'm so tired. Let's look over here.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I had been reading and thinking about what was happening in Gaza all the time, talking to people there. Every call with Banias was something I hadn't heard that was completely different from when adults tell the story.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So that is today's episode. We're calling it "The Narrator." We're going to listen to this kid in Gaza, a narrator who does not ask permission to narrate. She takes the phone with a soaring confidence that what she has to tell you is interesting and important, and I agree with her. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's This American Life. My calls with Banias were sporadic. Sometimes we talked once a week. Sometimes a month would go by. Usually, we talked at the end of the day, her time, while she was sitting on a mattress inside the house, fidgeting. There were always lots of people and activity in the background, but Banias never explained much about who was there or what they were doing. She told me about what she was doing, what she wanted me to know and sometimes see.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I prefer a video call.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: [BEEPING]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Let me try.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: This is my complete look.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's a good look.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She's in a pink shirt that says "Dream." Huge eyes, dark hair, and pigtails with two loose curls very purposefully framing her face.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And you have earrings. I didn't know you had earrings.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Oh, yeah, I do have earrings. And this is my blue shorts.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: And this, this is my head accessory for today. It has rhinestones.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Uh-huh. Purple, furry with rhinestones.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah, it's beautiful.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Banias and I first started talking on the phone, my questions were pretty basic. What do you do all day? She was in a house with 80 people, which is unusual in Gaza right now to live in a house. Most people are in tents or schools or other temporary shelters. Banias and her mom, dad, and baby brother were on the ground floor of this house, sharing that floor with about 20 relatives. There was one bedroom.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She slept on a mattress on the floor, alongside her parents, brother, grandpa, uncle, and aunt. Everyone else slept in the living area. If Banias wanted any time in the tiny bathroom, she got up early in the morning. Then she ate breakfast. And then what?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Today we play school games.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What does that mean?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: We're pretending that we're in the school. I was a student. And one of my friends was the teacher.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What classes were you taking?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Math class.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. And did you write actual math, or is it just pretend?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: It was actual, the plus and the minus and the equal. It was actual. But it was in a game, not real.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: At this point, July, Banias had not been in an actual class in an actual school building for nine months. But she played school every day with three other girls, two younger and one older. There were other kids in the building, but everyone else was just OK, or a boy, or a baby.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When aid organizations go into other war zones, one of the first things they do for kids is set up schools, because children need a sense of routine and a sense that life is moving forward toward a future. There's no safe place in Gaza to set up schools like that, so Banias and her friends in the building created that for themselves. They played school for hours. There were lectures. There were assignments. There were exams.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Who is usually in charge of what you're going to do that day?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: The girl that's older than me. Her name is Dana.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How old is Dana?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: She is 12 years old. And she has an iPad.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Dana is generous with her iPad. So this is another part of Banias's day-- games on the iPad. When the war started, her mother's screen time rules went out the window. But also, Israel cut off electricity to Gaza. There's just generators and solar panels, so screen time is limited anyway.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: And today, we played a cafe game.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, a cafe? That's new.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I was the chef. Yeah. And one of my friends was the customer. I cooked some salad and some pancake.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Say it one more time?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I cooked salad and pancake. And I made some hamburgers and some pizza.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Banias was re-enacting her old life, where she had teachers and exams and went out to cafes. There was one they used to go to every Saturday.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah, it was really close. It was just in the next street in our house.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK. Did they make salad and pancakes?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: No, but I used to order some noodles and some hot chocolate.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm. What did you eat in real life today?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Today we have eaten some beans, some white beans.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you ever get to eat pancakes or noodles or burgers?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I hate pancakes and noodles.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You do?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Do you believe somebody hates these things?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I do.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They're so good.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: But I hate them.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I was never sure what motivated Banias to want to talk to me. She seemed to like telling me about her day, practicing her English. She had an ongoing fascination with the time difference between us. She always wanted to check in on that.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: You're at morning or at night?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's the afternoon. It's just--

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Afternoon?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: We're in the middle of the night.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She'd call when she felt annoyed that Dana got to be the teacher that day yet again.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I am bored of being the student every day. I'm the oldest. I should be the teacher. Oof!

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And she'd call when she was bored. She'd call because I was an adult who would pay attention to her. Banias had to create activity-- interest-- out of such little material. Sometimes I got the impression I was there to help with that. Like, one night she was on the phone with me, and another phone rang. And like a character in a play, she went, oh, look, the phone is ringing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [PHONE RINGING]

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Oh, my God. Who's ringing the phone? Get away. Get lost.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: We have to sleep.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're pretty funny, Banias.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yes, I'm funny. Dana always say for me that I'm a bit funny.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Funny bunny.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm. You are funny.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yes. I'm a funny bunny.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So Banias had her own reasons to call me. When I called her, it was for different reasons. I'd call her because I'd read about a bombing campaign or fighting near where she was. Was she OK? And what was she thinking about all the violence around her? What is this like for an eight-year-old?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In the middle of the summer, there was a series of intense airstrikes near Banias. I was curious if she'd heard them or seen them, but I also wanted to follow her lead and what she wanted to talk about.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you have some time to talk?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Oh, yes, of course. I'm available.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Great.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I'm actually good.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Doing good. Last days, we have heard a bit of bombing around us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Uh-huh. Yeah, I've been reading in the news that there's been a lot of bombing.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah, I do know. It was loud.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Is it scary?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: No. For me, no. Me and my friends, we were playing hide-and-seek. We don't ever get bored of it. It's our favorite game. When we are playing, some strange things happens with us. I will tell you then.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK, I thought. Here it is. She's about to tell me something big about what it's like to be a kid playing hide-and-seek with bombs going off nearby. Banias told me, so we were playing, and we ran to the backyard.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: When we run to the backyard, we see some insects in the ground.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: We said, we see some insects on the ground. And me and the kids, we watched it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's it. That's her whole story. The strange thing that happened when they ran outside is they saw insects, a kind of insect they'd never seen before. Not the bombing-- bugs.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Children are not known for their sense of scale or the longevity of their attention. And maybe it wasn't surprising that pretty much every time I asked about the war, Banias didn't really want to engage. She didn't exactly ignore me, but it didn't seem to be the main thing she was thinking about.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like, when an airstrike broke the windows in her house, she wanted to tell me about a prank she played on Dana. In mid-August, when ceasefire negotiations between Israel and Hamas seemed to be unraveling yet again, and all the adults I was talking to in Gaza were deeply dispirited, here was Banias.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: I think there will be a ceasefire soon.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You do? Why do you think that?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Because it's really close to end.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Why? Why do you say-- what gives you that idea?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Mom and Dad tell me. [YAWNS]

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I heard that yawn-- noting it. Discussion of the war-- over. There was one moment when Banias was forced to engage. She couldn't avoid it. Banias's family had been sheltering in Deir Balah for almost a year, when, suddenly, at the end of August, they got an evacuation order. Israel posted a map on social media designating certain blocks in Deir Balah unsafe.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And I saw that Maram, Banias's mother, had written something for Al Jazeera about the order. I had hardly spoken to Maram for months, but I had followed her reporting on bombings and food shortages. This article, though, was personal. She wrote about her confusion about what to do next. "I've never felt so worthless as a human being," she wrote.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: "A single Facebook post from an Israeli military spokesperson can upend our lives in an instant. Have you ever felt like a toy being played with left and right, east and west, pushed from one place to another, south to Khan Younis, out of Rafah, back to Khan Younis, then to Nuseirat, only to be driven out again? People are literally running through the streets like mad, clutching what little they have left. We have nothing left. Our hearts are broken, and our minds are frayed.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I look around at the few possessions I've managed to gather over the past 10 months-- a stove, cups, plates, pots, winter clothes, summer clothes, mattresses, blankets, batteries, light bulbs, big bottles of drinking water, tubs to wash clothes in. If I leave everything, there's no way to replace it. There are no markets, no supplies, no money to spare. We're running and running aimlessly. People screaming, suffering, and dying while the world watches," end quote. And then my phone rang.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Hello?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Banias.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Do you want to talk?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Uh, OK. Today, we have done a new thing.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What'd you do?

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: We drawed some pictures. I imagined that there's a garden, that there's some people walking inside it.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: [CHILD CRYING]

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Stop crying. Go in the bedroom.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: So let's continue.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Banias
segments.text: Oh, my friends were with me, too, drawing. And one of my friends have drawed a plane.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Like a war plane or a plane you travel in?

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Disease in Gaza is widespread. Children face acute malnutrition. Kids are getting horrible skin infections. Polio has reappeared in a 10-month-old baby. Children are losing their limbs, their parents, and they are being killed, constantly. More than 13,000 children have been killed so far, including at least 710 babies, some of them born and then killed since the war began.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Chana Joffe-Walt, sitting in for Ira Glass. Our show today, "The Narrator," an eight-year-old in Gaza, tells us about her life in the middle of a war.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: This war started in 2023. Hamas attacked Israel, killed about 1,200 people, and took 251 people hostage. Since then, Israel has launched a 14-month ground invasion and bombing campaign in Gaza. More than 44,000 Palestinians have been killed, and more than 13,000 of those dead are children.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt

The dangers of moving into a tent could be worse than tanks outside their house. They decided to stay put. It was early October. The family was coming up on a year of war and displacement, and Banias had an announcement.

segments.text: There's something I've been thinking about when it comes to kids in wars, but kids in Gaza in particular. It's something a psychologist told me, Dr. Iman Farajallah, who studies the effect of war and occupation on Palestinian kids. She told me it really gets under her skin when people at the UN or healthcare professionals or whatever say kids in Gaza are suffering from PTSD.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Post-traumatic stress means the traumatic event is over. For kids in Gaza, the trauma is continuous. There is no post. There's no opportunity for recovery. Instead, there is just coping. Dr. Farajallah says, you'll see kids cope in all different ways. Some kids act out. Some can't leave their parents' side. Other kids get obsessed with soccer or drawing. Or children try to shape their world in other ways.

segments.text: Two days earlier, Israeli airstrikes hit Al Aqsa Hospital in Deir Balah, right near Banias's apartment. The hospital was surrounded by tents filled with displaced people sleeping. The airstrikes caused a fire that ripped through those tents. I'd seen Maram sharing images and videos of people sleeping in the tents burned alive.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I wondered if Banias had seen those images, but I didn't ask. Instead, we watched this Christmas movie. We watched Kevin trick the burglars into thinking his family is home by staging a fake party in his house.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Any war is a series of plot points. Even in an ongoing war, a never-ending and no-longer-new war, we track its progress by the worst moments. I kept calling Banias with this expectation, waiting for the story of the war as I was understanding it, to somehow intersect with her life as she was experiencing it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I kept imagining, dreading, that one of those moments will break through, that something bad will happen to Banias. One of those horrible plot points will become her plot point.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But something bad is happening to Banias. This is the plot point for her. She's sitting under the covers with no electricity, no heat, winter approaching. Banias has not been in school for over a year. She has no home. She has a cough, and there is no medicine.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Her friends have scattered. Some of them are dead. Her relatives are all over. Some of them are dead. She's eating canned beans, instead of burgers. She's finding glass in her brother's head. This is her life. This is the story she has to narrate.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: We have a couple minutes left in this episode, and I have a small update. Recently, Banias's family moved-- not far-- an apartment a couple miles from Deir Balah, where they've been staying. The new place is less crowded. There's more privacy for her family. It has trees outside and a refrigerator-- that doesn't work, but still. The apartment is quiet, temporary.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And it's not home. Banias knows she can't go home to the north of Gaza, where she's from. She knows her home was destroyed. She's seen pictures of her neighborhood exploded, on fire. And she's seen video of the empty space where her house was, the small mountains of rubble.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The gray couch with yellow cushions that she sat on after school, the chandelier her mother chose, the mirror by the door, the teacups and trays filled with treats, her new reimagined big girl bedroom with an Elsa bedspread, her desk, the pink moon they hung on the ceiling-- all of that is somewhere in that pile of rubble. All of that is there in the north of Gaza, their life.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But the north of Gaza has been transformed. There were about a million people living in northern Gaza when the war started, over 270,000 homes. Everyone was told to leave, to go south. Most people did. And now those people are separated from the north of Gaza by a wide militarized zone that they cannot cross.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Israel has been building and fortifying this military zone for the last few months. It cuts right across Gaza, splits Gaza in two, completely separating the north of Gaza, where Banias is from, from the south of Gaza, where she's been displaced to. This military zone is called the Netzarim Corridor. It has a constant military presence, and it's big, around 20 square miles. It takes up more than 12% of the entire territory of Gaza.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In order to build it, Israel cleared out a wide stretch of land, demolished hundreds of buildings, from the Israeli border all the way to the ocean. And in that space, Israel installed checkpoints and paved roads and flags and water lines and cell phone towers. It looks like something you'd put in place if you're planning to stay a while.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: A former chief of staff of the Israeli military has called the emptying out of the north of Gaza an ethnic cleansing. He said, quote, "the land is being cleared of Arabs." Human Rights Watch, Oxfam, Amnesty International have all called what is happening in Gaza an ethnic cleansing, or a genocide.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Israel denies this, and the Israeli military sent me a statement calling the charge of ethnic cleansing entirely baseless. It says it's working to dismantle Hamas's military infrastructure and is adhering to its obligations under international law.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The people who remained in the north and never left are under siege, with increasingly limited food and medical care. The UN says children are, quote, "as ever, the first and most to suffer."

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So this latest move for Banias's parents, it feels like a new phase. It's a move from "I can't believe it's gone on this long" to "this is going to keep going on." For Banias, it's more of the same, more temporary, more displacement, displacement that looks pretty likely to last most, if not all, of her childhood.
